case_study_insert.main_stem: Zephyr Precision Foundry (ZPF) is a private limited company in the aluminium casting sector, employing a workforce of 72. Founded in 2007 by Priya Zend, it die-casts aluminium housings for industrial machinery from its riverside plant and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZPF plans to invest $900,000 in a robotic die-casting cell, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $16 a unit and a selling price of $28, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. ZPF faces two operational problems: a scrap rate of 5.4% and high energy waste in the melting furnace.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The foundry cast 11,250 housings last quarter at a scrap rate of 5.4%, down from 7.1% a year earlier. Energy cost $48,000 a quarter and customer complaints fell from 41 to 24 a month. Delivery lead time is 6.3 days. A survey of 500 manufacturers found 66% would pay $0.75 more for low-carbon castings and 54% check environmental certification. Some 22 of the 72 operatives lack robotics training; a certification course costs $1,250 per operative.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zephyr Precision Foundry as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.40 to $14.14 an hour from April 2026, increasing total wage bills. (3) Aluminium input costs have risen 7.8% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 9.1%, and industrial output grew 2.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: ZPF plans to raise $300,000 through a share issue for its $900,000 robotic cell. Explain two advantages for ZPF of the share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings $300,000 that never has to be repaid and carries no interest, unlike the $600,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $360,000 a year and a scrap rate of 5.4%, ZPF can put every dollar of the $12 contribution per casting into covering costs and the 9.1% energy inflation rather than servicing more debt, improving the $900,000 project's chance of reaching its 45,000-unit target.

Point 2: New equity strengthens the balance sheet and leaves more of the borrowing capacity unused for the $600,000 loan already taken, which helps liquidity ratios and gives Priya Zend room to seek further finance if the robotic cell needs modifications. The 72-strong workforce and the 22 operatives needing robotics training can therefore be supported without raising loan interest; the cost is dilution of ownership and possible dividend pressure, but no fixed repayment is created. The $300,000 also spreads the risk of the $900,000 project among investors instead of leaving the downside with Priya Zend.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ZPF's investment, costs and financing.

questions.question_text: ZPF is promoting low-carbon castings to manufacturers. Consider sponsoring an engineering podcast, social-media influencer marketing, or a stand at an industrial trade fair. Which should ZPF choose to reach these buyers? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Sponsoring an engineering podcast: A podcast sponsorship reaches a loyal, technically qualified audience and can explain the low-carbon story in the sponsor's own words. It is relatively cheap against the $900,000 investment and suits a 72-employee foundry. However, reach is narrow and slow to build, there is no immediate enquiry data, and listeners may not be among the 500 manufacturers surveyed, so the message may miss buyers needing 6.3-day delivery.

Social-media influencer marketing: Influencers can create engaging content about recycled aluminium and reach younger engineers quickly with measurable clicks, supporting the 66% who would pay $0.75 more for low-carbon castings. The weakness is credibility: technical buyers may distrust influencers, and the 54% who check environmental certification need audited proof rather than social posts, so conversion into industrial orders may be weak.

Industrial trade fair stand: A trade fair gathers manufacturers, engineers and purchasing managers in one place, letting ZPF show certified low-carbon castings and discuss tolerances directly — important when 54% check certification. Leads are immediate and relationships can start there. Costs for stands and staff time are high, and results depend on which buyers attend, but the audience is far better matched than a general podcast or influencer campaign.

Recommendation: ZPF should choose an industrial trade fair stand as its main promotion. It delivers the face-to-face technical credibility that certification-focused buyers need and generates leads for a $900,000 robotic cell, which podcast reach and influencer clicks cannot match. Podcasts are rejected as too narrow and slow, and influencers are rejected as lacking the authority for audited low-carbon claims; a short podcast series can be used later to reinforce the message.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to ZPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZPF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of ZPF with a justified recommendation explaining why podcasts and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZPF has a 5.4% scrap rate and 22 operatives without robotics training. Explain two benefits for ZPF of using laissez-faire leadership with its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets experienced Operatives decide how best to run the die-casting cell, which suits a flat structure with 72 staff and can surface practical fixes for the 5.4% scrap rate faster than instructions from Priya Zend. Skilled operators who control their own routines are more likely to catch furnace faults early, protecting the 11,250 castings made each quarter and the $12 contribution on each one.

Point 2: Delegation frees senior managers to secure the $600,000 loan and the $300,000 share issue while operatives arrange their own cover for the $1,250 robotics certification course. This can raise ownership of quality and reduce energy waste in the melting furnace, because the people closest to the process choose when to adjust settings. The risk is that the 22 untrained staff may lack direction, so deadlines can slip if self-direction is not paired with clear standards. Delegation can also free managers to monitor the $48,000 a quarter energy bill, since operators closest to the furnace can report waste immediately.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZPF's scrap rate, training gap and structure.

questions.question_text: ZPF wants to cut its 5.4% scrap rate. Consider job rotation or job enrichment for the cell operatives. Which should ZPF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Job rotation: Moving operatives between melting, casting and inspection broadens their skills and reduces boredom, which can help the 22 staff without robotics training understand the whole process and spot faults causing the 5.4% scrap rate. Rotation also provides cover when someone attends the $1,250 certification course, keeping 11,250 castings a quarter on schedule. Its drawback is that frequent moves reduce practice on any one task and can raise errors during changeover, and it does not by itself give operators authority to stop a faulty batch.

Job enrichment: Giving operatives responsibility for quality checks and furnace settings, with feedback on scrap results, taps the flat structure and laissez-faire style and gives them a real stake in cutting the 7.1%-to-5.4% improvement further. It can raise motivation and ownership of the 9.1% energy-waste problem. The risk is that without training, the 22 unqualified staff may make poor setting decisions, and enrichment cannot fix a basic lack of robotics skill on the $900,000 cell.

Decision: ZPF should choose job enrichment supported by short rotation between casting and inspection. Enrichment gives the authority to reject faulty castings that a 5.4% scrap problem needs, and it fits the flat, delegated culture better than routine rotation. Rotation alone is rejected because it spreads staff thinly without ownership and can increase changeover errors; the $1,250 course should still be completed before operators take on settings responsibility. With 22 of 72 staff untrained, rotation can then be planned around course dates so the 11,250 castings a quarter are not disrupted.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two approaches with limited application to ZPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of ZPF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of ZPF with a justified decision covering skills, scrap and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZPF's management can use its cost and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($28 − $16) = $360,000 ÷ $12 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28 − $16 = $12. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZPF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 30,000 units against output of 45,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 15,000 units, showing how far orders can fall before the $900,000 robotic cell becomes a loss.
2. Contribution of $12 a casting lets managers test the survey premium: if 66% of buyers accept $0.75 more, contribution becomes $12.75, which can be weighed against the 7.8% aluminium input-cost rise before changing the $28 price.
3. The $600,000 bank loan can be evaluated against 30,000-unit break-even; above that point each casting adds $12, so managers can check the cell services interest before committing to the $300,000 share issue.
4. Unit cost ($360,000 ÷ 45,000 units + $16 = $24 a casting) benchmarks the 11,250 castings made last quarter and helps quantify the 5.4% scrap rate and the $48,000 quarterly energy bill, guiding furnace improvements.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 15,000 units; $0.75 premium modelling on $12 contribution; loan servicing on $600,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $24 to target the 5.4% scrap rate and $48,000 energy bill.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZPF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZPF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.68 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $350,000; 2025 current assets = $145,000 + $190,000 + $85,000 = $420,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $250,000 in both years gives 1.40 and 1.68. Excluding inventories: ($350,000 − $130,000) ÷ $250,000 = $220,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.88 in 2024, and ($420,000 − $145,000) ÷ $250,000 = $275,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.10 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved clearly. The current ratio rose from 1.40 to 1.68 as current assets grew $70,000 while current liabilities stayed at $250,000, helped by the $300,000 share issue. The stricter measure rose from 0.88 to 1.10, so by 2025 ZPF can cover short-term debts without depending on the sale of aluminium inventories — important while it services a $600,000 loan and runs a furnace using $48,000 of energy a quarter. However, trade receivables climbed from $160,000 to $190,000, so cash is tied up with manufacturers; if the 6.3-day delivery terms are followed by slow payment, the improvement could reverse, and inventories at $145,000 also need watching given the 5.4% scrap rate.

Conclusion: ZPF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the stricter test now exceeds 1, so the gain is not stock-dependent. Cash of $85,000 in 2025 is a useful buffer for the $600,000 loan. The main risk is growing receivables, so credit control should be tightened before further investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZPF of introducing more robotics on its die-casting cell.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Robots can repeat pours and extracts precisely, cutting the 5.4% scrap rate and the $48,000 a quarter energy waste by shortening furnace idle time. More consistent castings protect the $12 contribution on each of the 11,250 units made a quarter and support the low-carbon castings that 66% of surveyed manufacturers would pay $0.75 more for, strengthening the case for the $900,000 investment.

Disadvantage: Robots need programming and maintenance skills, yet 22 of the 72 operatives lack robotics training and the $1,250 certification course is an extra cost. A breakdown could stop the whole cell, losing output and contribution, and the flat laissez-faire structure may delay decisions if nobody owns the machine. With $600,000 already borrowed, a further automation failure would strain liquidity. The flat laissez-faire structure may also leave no one accountable for maintenance, so a robot fault could idle the $900,000 cell and delay the 6.3-day delivery promise; the $1,250 course helps but does not remove that dependency.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZPF's scrap rate, training gap and finance.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 7.8% rise in aluminium input costs will affect ZPF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): The increase is 5.50% − 4.75% = 0.75 percentage points. If the $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest = 0.75% × $600,000 = 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year. This is small next to fixed costs of $360,000 and the $48,000 a quarter energy bill, and it disappears entirely if the loan is fixed. The higher rate may discourage the $300,000 share issue investors, but the direct cash effect is limited.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, $13.40 to $14.14 an hour): ZPF has a workforce of 72 and produces 45,000 units, so labour productivity = 45,000 ÷ 72 = 625 castings per worker. The insert supplies no hours worked and no individual wage, so a total annual wage bill cannot be derived honestly. The rise is unavoidable and will raise unit labour cost unless productivity holds at 625 per worker; otherwise the $12 contribution per casting falls, but the size of the effect cannot be quantified from the data given.

Aluminium input-cost inflation (7.8%): The insert does not break down the $16 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if the whole $16 rose by 7.8%, the increase = 7.8% × $16 = 0.078 × $16 = $1.248 a casting; across 45,000 units that is 45,000 × $1.248 = $56,160 a year. Combined with 9.1% energy inflation, this hits every casting and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate.

Conclusion: The 7.8% rise in aluminium input costs will have the greatest impact. It erodes the $12 contribution on all 45,000 castings, with a computable upper-bound exposure of $56,160 a year, far above the $4,500 interest effect, while the wage impact cannot even be quantified from the insert. Management should renegotiate aluminium supply and pursue the $0.75 low-carbon premium before accepting higher borrowing costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to ZPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ZPF's costs, revenue or financing with figures derived from the insert.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with shown derivations and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
